english: It flattered Tansley. After being snubbed, he found it soothing that Mrs. Ramsay should confide this to him. Charles Tansley perked up. She suggested, too, how great a man’s intellect was, even as it declined, and how every wife was subordinate to her husband’s work—not that she blamed the girl, and the marriage had been happy enough, she believed—and this made him more pleased with himself than he had been so far. He would have liked, say, if they had taken a cab, to be the one to pay. And her little bag—might he carry it? No, no, she said, she always carried _that_ herself. And she did, too. Yes, he could sense that about her. He sensed a great many things, one thing especially that excited and unsettled him for reasons he could not put into words. He wanted her to see him in academic cap and gown, walking in a procession. A fellowship, a professorship—he felt he could do anything, and pictured himself—but what was she looking at? A man pasting up a poster. The enormous flapping sheet smoothed itself flat, and every sweep of the brush uncovered more legs, hoops, horses, gleaming reds and blues, beautifully sleek, until half the wall was taken up by a circus advertisement: a hundred horsemen, twenty performing seals, lions, tigers. … Leaning forward, because she was shortsighted, she read aloud that it … “will visit this town.” What terribly dangerous work, she exclaimed, for a man with one arm to stand at the top of a ladder like that—he had lost his left arm in a reaping machine two years ago.

Han ville gerne, hvis de havde taget en droske, have været den, der betalte. Og hendes lille taske — måtte han bære den? Nej, nej, sagde hun, _den_ bar hun altid selv. Og det gjorde hun også. Ja, det kunne han fornemme ved hende. Han fornemmede mange ting, én ting især, der ophidsede og forvirrede ham af grunde, han ikke kunne sætte ord på. Han ønskede, hun skulle se ham i akademisk hue og kappe, gående i procession. Et stipendium, et professorat — han følte, han kunne alt, og forestillede sig selv — men hvad så hun på? En mand, der klistrede en plakat op. Det enorme flagrende ark glattede sig ud, og hvert strøg med kosten afdækkede flere ben, bøjler, heste, funklende røde og blå farver, smukt glatte, indtil halvdelen af muren var optaget af en cirkusannonce: hundrede ryttere, tyve optrædende sæler, løver, tigre. … Hun lænede sig frem, fordi hun var nærsynet, og læste højt, at den … »besøger denne by«. english: The clematis was a bright violet; the wall was a staring white. Since that was how she saw them, she would not have thought it honest to tamper with them, even though it had been the fashion, ever since Mr. Paunceforte came, to see everything as pale, elegant, half-transparent. And then, beneath the color, there was the shape. When she looked, she could see it all so clearly, so commandingly. It was when she picked up her brush that everything changed. In that moment’s flight between the picture and the canvas the demons fell on her—the demons who often brought her close to tears, and made this passage from idea to work as frightening as a dark corridor is to a child. That was often how she felt: fighting against terrible odds to keep her courage up, to say, “But this is what I see; this is what I see,” and so to hug to her breast some miserable scrap of her vision, while a thousand forces did their best to tear it away. And it was then too, as she started to paint, in that chill and windy way, that other things pushed in on her: how inadequate she was, how insignificant, keeping house for her father off the Brompton Road. She could barely control the impulse to throw herself (thank Heaven she had always resisted so far) at Mrs. Ramsay’s knee and tell her—but what could anyone tell her? “I’m in love with you?” No, that wasn’t true. “I’m in love with all this,” with a wave of her hand at the hedge, the house, the children? english: “It suddenly gets cold. The sun seems to give less heat,” she said, glancing around, for it was still bright enough. The grass kept its soft deep green; purple passionflowers starred the greenery on the house; and from the high blue, rooks let fall their cool cries. But something moved and flashed; a silver wing turned in the air. It was September, after all—mid-September—and it was past six in the evening. So they wandered off down the garden the usual way, by the tennis lawn and the pampas grass, to the gap in the thick hedge. Red-hot pokers guarded it like braziers of clear burning coal, and between them the blue water of the bay looked bluer than ever.

english: The Ramsays weren’t rich, and how they managed it all was a wonder. Eight children! Eight children fed on philosophy! And here came another one, Jasper this time, wandering by to take a shot at a bird, as he put it casually, and pumping Lily’s hand like a pump handle on his way past, so that Mr. Bankes said bitterly how _she_ was a favorite. Now there was schooling to think about (though true, Mrs. Ramsay perhaps had a little money of her own), to say nothing of the everyday wear and tear on the shoes and stockings of those “great fellows,” well-grown, angular, ruthless young things every one of them. As for telling them apart, or knowing the order they came in, he couldn’t. In private he named them after the kings and queens of England: Cam the Wicked, James the Ruthless, Andrew the Just, Prue the Fair—because Prue would be beautiful, he thought, how could she not be?—and Andrew would have brains. Walking up the drive, while Lily Briscoe said yes and no and capped his remarks (she was in love with them all, in love with this world), he weighed up Ramsay’s case. He felt sorry for him; he envied him. It was as though he had watched Ramsay shed all the glories of isolation and austerity that crowned him as a young man, and load himself for good with fluttering wings and clucking domestic life. They gave him something—William Bankes granted that. It would have been nice if Cam had stuck a flower in his buttonhole, or climbed over his shoulder the way she climbed over her father’s, to look at a picture of Vesuvius erupting. But his old friends couldn’t help feeling that they had also destroyed something. What would a stranger make of him now? What did this Lily Briscoe make of him? Who could fail to notice that habits were growing on him—eccentricities, perhaps weaknesses? That a man with his intellect could sink so low—no, the phrase was too harsh—could lean so heavily on other people’s praise: that was astonishing.
danish_before_fix: Familien Ramsay var ikke rig, og hvordan de klarede det hele, var et under. Otte børn! Otte børn fodret med filosofi! Og her kom endnu et, Jasper denne gang, der slentrede forbi for at skyde efter en fugl, som han sagde henkastet, og pumpede Lilys hånd som en pumpesvingel på vej forbi, så hr. Bankes bittert sagde, at _hun_ var en favorit. Nu var der skolegang at tænke på (selv om fru Ramsay sandt at sige måske havde lidt penge af sig selv), for ikke at tale om det daglige slid på sko og strømper på de »store fyre«, velvoksne, kantede, hensynsløse unge væsener hver eneste af dem. At skelne dem fra hinanden eller kende rækkefølgen, de kom i, kunne han ikke. I det stille opkaldte han dem efter Englands konger og dronninger: Cam den Onde, James den Hensynsløse, Andrew den Retfærdige, Prue den Skønne — for Prue ville blive smuk, mente han, hvordan kunne hun andet? — og Andrew ville få hjerne. Mens han gik op ad indkørslen, og Lily Briscoe sagde ja og nej og tog hans bemærkninger op (hun var forelsket i dem alle, forelsket i denne verden), afvejede han Ramsays sag. Han ynkede ham; han misundte ham. Det var, som om han havde set Ramsay lægge al den ensomheds og strenghedens glans fra sig, som kronede ham som ung, og for stedse læsse sig til med flagrende vinger og kluksende husliv. De gav ham noget — det indrømmede William Bankes. Det ville have været rart, hvis Cam havde stukket en blomst i hans knaphul eller var kravlet over hans skulder, som hun kravlede over sin fars, for at se på et billede af Vesuvs udbrud. Men hans gamle venner kunne ikke lade være med at føle, at de også havde ødelagt noget. Hvad ville en fremmed tænke om ham nu? Hvad tænkte denne Lily Briscoe om ham? Hvem kunne undgå at lægge mærke til, at vaner var ved at tage overhånd hos ham — særheder, måske svagheder? At en mand med hans intellekt kunne synke så lavt — nej, udtrykket var for hårdt — kunne læne sig så tungt op ad andres ros: det var forbløffende.

english: So whenever Mr. Ramsay’s work came to mind, what she saw was a scrubbed kitchen table. Just now it sat lodged in the fork of a pear tree, since they had come into the orchard. With a painful effort she concentrated her mind—not on the tree’s silver-studded bark, nor on its leaves shaped like fish, but on a phantom kitchen table stuck up there with its four legs in the air: one of those scrubbed plank tables, grained and knotted, whose virtue seems to have been laid bare by years of muscular honesty. Naturally, if you spent your days seeing angular essences like this, shrinking lovely evenings, with all their flamingo clouds and their blue and silver, down to a four-legged table of white pine (and the finest minds did exactly that), naturally you could not be judged like other people.

Med en smertefuld anstrengelse samlede hun tankerne — ikke om træets sølvbeslåede bark eller dets fiskeformede blade, men om et fantombord, der sad fast deroppe med fire ben i vejret: et af de skrubbede plankeborde, åreforede og knastede, hvis dyd synes at være blevet blottet af års muskuløs ærlighed. english: Not for the world would she have spoken to him. She knew the signs: his eyes turned away, and a curious gathering-in of his whole person, as if he were wrapping himself up and needed privacy in which to get his balance back. They told her he was outraged and in anguish. She stroked James’s head; she passed on to him what she felt for her husband. As she watched him color the white dress shirt of a gentleman in the Army and Navy Stores catalogue yellow with his chalk, she thought what a delight it would be to her if he turned out to be a great artist; and why shouldn’t he? He had a splendid forehead. Then, looking up as her husband passed her once more, she was relieved to find that the ruin was veiled. Domestic life had won; habit was crooning its soothing rhythm. So when he stopped deliberately at the window as his turn came round again, and bent down, teasing and whimsical, to tickle James’s bare calf with a sprig of something, she scolded him lightly for having sent off “that poor young man,” Charles Tansley. Tansley had had to go in and write his dissertation, he said.

english: Mrs. Ramsay could have wished her husband hadn’t picked that moment to stop. Why hadn’t he gone off to watch the children play cricket, as he’d said he would? But he said nothing; he looked; he nodded; he approved; he moved on. Before him he saw the hedge that had so many times rounded off a pause, signaled a conclusion; he saw his wife and child; he saw once more the urns with their trailing red geraniums, which had so often decorated his processes of thought and which bore them written up among their leaves, like scraps of paper you scribble notes on in the rush of reading. Seeing all this, he slid smoothly into speculation prompted by an article in _The Times_ on how many Americans visit Shakespeare’s house each year. Had Shakespeare never existed, he asked, would the world be much different from the way it is now? Does civilization advance because of great men? Is the ordinary person better off now than under the Pharaohs? And yet, he asked himself, is the ordinary person’s lot the right yardstick for measuring civilization? Possibly not. Possibly the greatest good depends on there being a slave class. The man who operates the lift in the Underground will always be necessary. He found the thought distasteful. He tossed his head. To escape it, he would find a way to take the arts down a peg. He would argue that the world exists for the ordinary person; that the arts are just ornament laid on top of human life; they do not express it. Nor does life need Shakespeare. Without knowing quite why he wanted to run Shakespeare down and to rescue the man who stands forever in the door of the lift, he snapped a leaf off the hedge. All this would have to be served up for the young men at Cardiff next month, he thought; out here on his terrace he was only foraging and picnicking (he tossed away the leaf he had picked so peevishly), like a man leaning down from his horse to gather a bunch of roses, or filling his pockets with nuts as he ambles comfortably through the lanes and fields of the countryside he has known since he was a boy. All of it was familiar: this bend, that stile, that path across the fields. He would spend hours this way in the evenings, with his pipe, thinking his way up and down and in and out of the old familiar lanes and commons, which were all dotted with the history of that campaign over there, the life of this statesman here, with poems and anecdotes, and with figures too, this thinker, that soldier; everything brisk and clear. But eventually the lane, the field, the common, the fruitful nut tree and the flowering hedge brought him to that further bend in the road where he always dismounted, tied his horse to a tree, and went on alone, on foot. He came to the edge of the lawn and gazed out over the bay below.

Havde Shakespeare aldrig eksisteret, spurgte han, ville verden da være meget anderledes, end den er nu? Skrider civilisationen frem på grund af store mænd? Har almindelige mennesker det bedre nu end under faraoerne? Og alligevel, spurgte han sig selv, er det almindelige menneskes lod det rette mål at måle civilisationen med? Måske ikke. Måske afhænger det største gode af, at der findes en slaveklasse. Manden, der betjener elevatoren i undergrundsbanen, vil altid være nødvendig. Han fandt tanken usmagelig. Han kastede med hovedet. For at slippe fra den ville han finde en måde at få kunsten sat på plads. Han ville hævde, at verden eksisterer for det almindelige menneske; at kunsten blot er pynt, lagt oven på menneskelivet; den udtrykker det ikke. Livet har heller ikke brug for Shakespeare. Uden helt at vide, hvorfor han ville rakke Shakespeare ned og redde manden, der evigt står i elevatorens dør, rev han et blad af hækken. Alt dette skulle serveres for de unge mænd i Cardiff næste måned, tænkte han; herude på sin terrasse var han kun ved at fouragere og holde picnic (han smed det blad væk, han så gnavent havde plukket), som en mand, der læner sig ned fra sin hest for at samle en buket roser eller fylder lommerne med nødder, mens han spadserer behageligt af sted gennem de veje og marker i landskabet, han har kendt, siden han var dreng. Alt var velkendt: dette sving, hint led, den sti over markerne. Sådan ville han bruge timer om aftenen, med sin pibe, og tænke sig op og ned og ind og ud af de gamle velkendte veje og fælleder, der alle var oversået med historien om hint felttog derovre, denne statsmands liv her, med digte og anekdoter, og med skikkelser også, denne tænker, hin soldat; alt sammen livligt og klart. Men til sidst bragte vejen, marken, fællesen, det frugtbare nøddetræ og den blomstrende hæk ham til det yderligere sving, hvor han altid steg af, bandt sin hest til et træ og gik videre alene, til fods. Han nåede til kanten af plænen og stirrede ud over bugten nedenfor.

english: ‘Well, what does she want, then?’ said the Flounder.” And where had they got to by now? Mrs. Ramsay wondered. She could read and think at once with no trouble at all, for the story of the Fisherman and his Wife was like a bass line quietly accompanying a tune, now and then running up without warning into the melody. And when was she going to be told? If nothing had happened, she would have to have a serious talk with Minta. Minta simply couldn’t go tramping all over the countryside, even with Nancy along (once more she tried, and failed, to picture their backs going down the path, and to count them). She was answerable to Minta’s parents—the Owl and the Poker. Her nicknames for them flashed into her mind as she read. The Owl and the Poker—yes, they would be displeased if they heard (and they were sure to hear) that Minta, while staying with the Ramsays, had been seen et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. “He wore a wig in the House of Commons and she ably assisted him at the head of the stairs,” she said over to herself, hauling them up out of her memory with a phrase she had invented, on the way home from some party, to amuse her husband. Dear me, Mrs. Ramsay said to herself, how had those two ever produced such an unlikely daughter? This tomboy Minta, with a hole in her stocking? How did she survive in that ponderous atmosphere, where the maid was forever sweeping into a dustpan the sand the parrot had scattered, and conversation had shrunk almost entirely to that bird’s exploits—interesting, perhaps, but limited, when all was said and done? Naturally she had invited Minta to lunch, then tea, then dinner, and in the end to come and stay with them up at Finlay. That had caused some friction with the Owl, her mother, and led to more calls, and more conversation, and more sand, until, by the end of it, she had told enough lies about parrots to last a lifetime (as she had put it to her husband that night, on the way home from the party). Still, Minta came. … Yes, she had come, Mrs. Ramsay thought, feeling some thorn caught in the tangle of this thought; and when she worked it loose, she found that it was this. A woman had once accused her of “robbing her of her daughter’s affections”; and something Mrs. Doyle had said brought that accusation back to her. That she wanted to dominate, wanted to interfere, made people do what she wanted—that was the charge against her, and she thought it deeply unfair. How could she help looking “like that”? Nobody could say she went to any trouble to impress. She was often ashamed of how shabby she was. Nor was she domineering, nor tyrannical. It was truer where hospitals and drains and the dairy were concerned. About things like that she did feel passionately, and, given the chance, she would have liked to grab people by the scruff of the neck and make them see. Not one hospital on the whole island. It was a disgrace. Milk left on your doorstep in London that was actually brown with dirt. There ought to be a law against it. A model dairy and a hospital here—those were the two things she would have liked to do, with her own hands. But how? With all these children? Later, when they were older, maybe she would have time; once they were all at school.

Og hvornår skulle hun få det at vide? Hvis intet var sket, måtte hun have en alvorlig samtale med Minta. Minta kunne simpelthen ikke traske rundt i hele egnen, selv om Nancy var med (endnu en gang forsøgte hun at se deres ryg gå ned ad stien og at tælle dem, og det lykkedes ikke). Hun havde ansvaret over for Mintas forældre — Uglen og Ildjernet. Hendes øgenavne til dem blinkede op i hende, mens hun læste. Uglen og Ildjernet — ja, de ville blive misfornøjede, hvis de hørte (og det ville de helt sikkert), at Minta, mens hun boede hos Ramsays, var blevet set og så videre, og så videre, og så videre. »Han bar paryk i Underhuset, og hun assisterede ham dygtigt øverst på trappen,« sagde hun hen for sig selv og halede dem op af hukommelsen med en vending, hun havde fundet på på vej hjem fra en eller anden fest for at more sin mand. Du milde, sagde fru Ramsay til sig selv, hvordan i alverden havde de to kunnet få en så usandsynlig datter? Den her drengepige Minta, med hul på strømpen? Hvordan overlevede hun i den tunge atmosfære, hvor stuepigen evigt fejede sandet, som papegøjen havde spredt, op på en fejebakke, og samtalen næsten helt var skrumpet ind til den fugls bedrifter — interessante, måske, men begrænsede, når alt kom til alt? Naturligvis havde hun inviteret Minta til frokost, så til te, så til middag, og til sidst til at komme og bo hos dem oppe på Finlay. Det havde forårsaget en vis gnidning med Uglen, hendes mor, og ført til flere besøg og mere konversation og mere sand, indtil hun til sidst havde fortalt nok løgne om papegøjer til at række et helt liv (som hun havde udtrykt det over for sin mand den aften, på vej hjem fra festen). Alligevel kom Minta. … Ja, hun var kommet, tænkte fru Ramsay og mærkede en torn sidde fast i denne tankes filtrede nøgle; og da hun fik den løsnet, fandt hun, at det var dette. En kvinde havde engang beskyldt hende for »at røve hende hendes datters hengivenhed«; og noget, fru Doyle havde sagt, havde bragt den beskyldning tilbage for hende. At hun ville dominere, ville blande sig, fik folk til at gøre, som hun ville — det var anklagen mod hende, og hun fandt den dybt uretfærdig. Hvordan kunne hun gøre for, at hun så ud »sådan«? Ingen kunne sige, at hun gjorde sig nogen anstrengelser for at imponere. Hun skammede sig ofte over, hvor lasket hun så ud. Hun var heller ikke herskesyg eller tyrannisk. Det passede bedre, når det gjaldt hospitaler og kloakker og mejeriet. Om den slags følte hun virkelig lidenskabeligt, og hvis hun fik chancen, ville hun have grebet folk i nakkeskindet og tvunget dem til at se. Ikke ét eneste hospital på hele øen. Det var en skam. Mælk, der blev stillet uden for din dør i London, og som faktisk var brun af snavs. Det burde være forbudt ved lov. Et mønstermejeri og et hospital her — det var de to ting, hun gerne ville have gjort, med sine egne hænder. Men hvordan? Med alle de børn? Senere, når de var større, ville hun måske få tid; når de alle var kommet i skole.

english: What made her say that: “We are in the hands of the Lord”? she wondered. That insincerity, slipping in among the truths, stirred and annoyed her. She took up her knitting once more. How could any Lord have made this world? she asked. Her mind had always grasped the fact that there is no reason, no order, no justice—only suffering, death, the poor. The world would stoop to any betrayal, however low; she knew that. Happiness never lasted; she knew that. Firm and composed, she knitted, lips slightly pursed, and without realizing it she had set the lines of her face into such a habit of sternness that her husband, walking past, couldn’t help noticing it: the sternness at the heart of her beauty. He was chuckling as he passed, at the thought of Hume, the philosopher, grown enormously fat and stuck in a bog. But her look saddened him; her remoteness hurt him; going by, he felt he couldn’t protect her, and by the time he got to the hedge, he was sad. There was nothing he could do for her. He had to stand by and watch her. The damnable truth, in fact, was that he made things worse for her. He was irritable—he was touchy. He had lost his temper over the Lighthouse. He stared into the hedge, into its tangle, its darkness.

english: They had come to the gap between the two clumps of red-hot pokers, and there was the Lighthouse again, but she wouldn’t allow herself to look at it. Had she known he was watching her, she thought, she would never have let herself sit there thinking. She disliked anything that reminded her she had been seen sitting and thinking. So she glanced back over her shoulder at the town. Its lights rippled and ran like drops of silver water held steady in a wind. And all the poverty, all the suffering, had turned into that, thought Mrs. Ramsay. The lights of the town, the harbor, and the boats looked like a phantom net floating there to mark the place where something had sunk. Well, if he couldn’t share her thoughts, Mr. Ramsay told himself, then he’d go off on his own. He wanted to keep thinking, to keep telling himself the story of Hume stuck in a bog; he wanted to laugh. But first, it was nonsense to worry about Andrew. At Andrew’s age he used to tramp about the countryside all day with nothing but a biscuit in his pocket, and nobody fretted about him or imagined he had fallen off a cliff. Aloud he said he thought he might go off for a day’s walk, if the weather held. He’d had just about enough of Bankes and Carmichael. He’d like a little solitude. Yes, she said. There were little sandy beaches where nobody had been since the beginning of time. The seals sat up and stared at you. Sometimes it seemed to him that in a little house out there, by himself—he broke off with a sigh. He had no right. The father of eight children—he reminded himself of that. And he’d have been a brute and a cur to wish one thing different. Andrew would turn out a better man than he had. Prue would be a beauty, her mother said. They would hold back the flood a little. On the whole, that was a good piece of work—his eight children. They proved he didn’t utterly damn the poor little universe; for on an evening like this, he thought, watching the land fade away, the little island looked pitifully small, half swallowed by the sea.

english: She had been to Brussels; she had been to Paris, though only on a quick trip to visit a sick aunt. She had been to Dresden; there were masses of pictures she’d never seen; but perhaps, Lily Briscoe reflected, it was better not to see pictures: all they did was make you hopelessly dissatisfied with your own work. Mr. Bankes felt you could take that view too far. We can’t all be Titians and we can’t all be Darwins, he said; yet he doubted whether there could be any Darwin or Titian without humble people like ourselves. Lily wanted to pay him a compliment; you’re not humble, Mr. Bankes, she would have liked to say. But he didn’t want compliments (most men do, she thought), and a little ashamed of the impulse, she kept quiet while he remarked that perhaps what he’d said didn’t apply to pictures. At any rate, said Lily, dashing off her small insincerity, she would always keep on painting, because it interested her. Yes, Mr. Bankes said, he was sure of that. As they came to the end of the lawn he was asking whether she found it hard to find subjects in London, when they turned and saw the Ramsays. So that is marriage, Lily thought: a man and a woman watching a girl throw a ball. That is what Mrs. Ramsay was trying to tell me the other night, she thought. For Mrs. Ramsay had on a green shawl, and the two stood close together, watching Prue and Jasper throw catches. And suddenly the meaning that comes down on people for no reason at all—as they’re stepping out of the Underground, perhaps, or ringing a doorbell—and makes them symbolic, makes them representative, came down on these two, and turned them, standing and gazing in the dusk, into the symbols of marriage, husband and wife. Then, after an instant, the symbolic outline that rose above the real figures sank again, and as Lily and Mr. Bankes came up to them they were simply Mr. and Mrs. Ramsay watching the children throw catches. Yet for a moment still—though Mrs. Ramsay greeted them with her usual smile (oh, she thinks we’re going to get married, Lily thought) and said, “I’ve triumphed tonight,” meaning that for once Mr. Bankes had agreed to have dinner with them rather than hurrying back to his lodgings, where his manservant cooked vegetables the proper way—still, for a single moment, there was a feeling of things blown apart, of space, of irresponsibility, as the ball soared up, and their eyes followed it and lost it and found the one star and the draped branches. In the fading light they all looked sharp-edged and unearthly and set apart by great distances. Then, dashing backward across the huge space (for solidity seemed to have vanished completely), Prue ran full tilt into them and brilliantly caught the ball high up in her left hand; and her mother said, “Aren’t they back yet?” and at that the spell broke. Now Mr. Ramsay felt free to laugh out loud at Hume, who had got stuck in a bog and was rescued by an old woman on condition that he said the Lord’s Prayer; and chuckling to himself, he wandered off to his study. Så, efter et øjeblik, sank den symbolske kontur, der havde hævet sig over de virkelige skikkelser, igen, og da Lily og hr. Bankes nåede hen til dem, var de bare hr. og fru Ramsay, der så på børnene, der kastede bold. english: “A disaster,” agreed Paul, leaping to his feet; and as they slid and scrambled down, he kept quoting the guidebook about “these islands being justly celebrated for their park-like prospects and the extent and variety of their marine curiosities.” But it wasn’t quite right, Andrew felt, picking his way down the cliff—all this shouting and damning your eyes, this slapping him on the back and calling him “old fellow” and the rest of it; it wasn’t quite right. That was the trouble with taking women on walks. On the beach they split up. Andrew went out onto the Pope’s Nose, took off his shoes, rolled his socks up inside them, and left that couple to look after themselves; Nancy waded out to rocks of her own and searched pools of her own and left that couple to look after themselves. Crouching low, she touched the smooth, rubbery sea anemones that clung like lumps of jelly to the side of the rock. Brooding, she made the pool into the sea, and the minnows into sharks and whales; she held her hand up against the sun and threw vast clouds over this tiny world, bringing darkness and desolation, like God himself, to millions of ignorant, innocent creatures; then all at once she pulled her hand away and let the sunlight pour down. Across the pale crisscrossed sand stalked some fantastic leviathan, high-stepping, fringed, gauntleted (she was still making the pool bigger), and slid into the vast cracks of the mountainside. And then, as her eyes slid imperceptibly up above the pool and came to rest on the wavering line where sea met sky, on the tree trunks that steamer smoke set wavering on the horizon, all that power sweeping savagely in and inevitably pulling back held her hypnotized. And the two sensations, of that hugeness and of this tininess (the pool had shrunk again), flowering inside it, made her feel tied hand and foot, unable to move, under the intensity of feelings that shrank her own body, her own life, and the lives of everyone in the world, forever, to nothing. So she brooded, crouched over the pool, listening to the waves.

english: Only when they had climbed all the way back to the top of the cliff did Minta cry out that she had lost her grandmother’s brooch—her grandmother’s brooch, the one ornament she owned—a weeping willow (they must remember it) set in pearls. She would rather have lost anything else! She was going back to look for it. They all went back. They poked about and peered and searched. They kept their heads down low and spoke in short, gruff bursts. Paul Rayley hunted like a madman all around the rock where they’d been sitting. All this fuss over a brooch really wasn’t right at all, Andrew thought, while Paul told him to make a “thorough search between this point and that.” The tide was rising fast. In a minute the sea would be over the spot where they’d sat. There wasn’t a ghost of a chance they’d find it now. “We’ll be cut off!” Minta shrieked, suddenly terrified. As if there were the least danger of that! It was the bulls all over again—she couldn’t control her feelings, Andrew thought. Women couldn’t. Poor Paul had to calm her. The men (Andrew and Paul at once turned manly and unlike their usual selves) held a brief council and decided to stick Rayley’s cane in the ground where they’d been sitting and return at low tide. For now, nothing more could be done. If the brooch was there, it would still be there in the morning, they promised her; yet Minta went on sobbing all the way to the top of the cliff. Then Minta Doyle, who had good instincts, declared bluntly and absurdly that she didn’t believe anybody truly enjoyed reading Shakespeare. Very few people, Mr. Ramsay said grimly (though his mind had turned away again), liked it as much as they claimed. He would laugh at Minta; and Minta, Mrs. Ramsay saw, sensing how intensely anxious he was about himself, would make sure in her own way that he was looked after, and would praise him somehow. But she wished it weren’t necessary; perhaps it was her own fault that it was. english: she read, and turned the page, and swung herself, zigzagging here and there, from line to line as if from branch to branch, from one red and white flower to the next, until she was roused by a small sound—her husband slapping his thighs. For a second their eyes met; but neither wanted to talk. There was nothing to say, and still something seemed to pass between them, from him to her. It was the life of the book, its power, its enormous humor, she knew, that made him slap his thighs. Don’t interrupt, he seemed to be telling her; don’t speak; just sit. And he read on. His lips twitched. It filled him up. It gave him strength. All the petty irritations and jabs of the evening went clean out of his head—how unbearably dull he found it to sit still while people went on eating and drinking forever, how snappish he had been with his wife, how thin-skinned, how he had minded when they skipped over his books as if they did not exist. english: So, guided by some stray light from an uncovered star, or a wandering ship, or even the Lighthouse, with its pale footfall on stair and mat, the little breaths of air climbed the staircase and nosed around the bedroom doors. But here, surely, they must stop. Whatever else may perish and disappear, what lies here is steadfast. Here you might say to those sliding lights, those fumbling airs that breathe and bend over the bed itself: here you can neither touch nor destroy. At which, wearily, ghostlike, as if they had feather-light fingers and the light persistence of feathers, they would look once at the shut eyes and the loosely clasped fingers, and wearily fold their garments and disappear. And so, nosing, rubbing, they went to the window on the staircase, to the servants’ bedrooms, to the boxes in the attics; coming down again, they whitened the apples on the dining-room table, fumbled at the petals of the roses, tried the picture on the easel, brushed the mat and blew a little sand along the floor. english: As she lurched (for she rolled like a ship at sea) and leered (for her eyes never fell on anything directly, but only with a sidelong glance that asked to be spared the scorn and anger of the world—she was witless, she knew it), as she clutched the banisters and hauled herself upstairs and rolled from room to room, she sang. Rubbing the glass of the long mirror and leering sideways at her swaying figure, she let a sound come from her lips—something that had perhaps been cheerful on the stage twenty years before, had been hummed and danced to, but now, coming from this toothless, bonneted caretaker, was robbed of meaning. It was like the voice of witlessness, of humor, of persistence itself, trodden down but springing up again; so that as she lurched along, dusting, wiping, she seemed to be saying how it was all one long sorrow and trouble, how it was getting up and going to bed again, and getting things out and putting them away again. It had not been easy or cozy, this world she had known for close on seventy years. She was bowed down with weariness. How long, she asked, creaking and groaning on her knees under the bed, dusting the boards, how long is it to go on? But she hobbled to her feet again, pulled herself up, and again, with her sidelong leer that slipped and turned aside even from her own face and her own sorrows, stood and gaped in the glass, smiling at nothing, and began again the old amble and hobble, taking up mats, putting down china, looking sideways in the glass—as if, after all, she had her consolations; as if some incorrigible hope really did twine itself around her dirge. There must have been visions of joy at the washtub, say, with her children (though two had been born out of wedlock and one had deserted her), or at the pub, drinking, or turning over odds and ends in her drawers. There must have been some break in the dark, some channel in the depths of obscurity through which enough light came to twist her face into a grin in the glass, and make her, turning to her work again, mumble out the old music-hall song. Meanwhile the mystics, the visionaries, walked the beach, stirred a puddle, looked at a stone, and asked themselves, “What am I?” “What is this?”—and suddenly an answer was granted them (what it was they could not say), so that they were warm in the frost and had comfort in the desert. But Mrs. McNab went on drinking and gossiping as before.

english: As summer drew near and the evenings lengthened, the wakeful and the hopeful who walked the beach and stirred the pools began to have the strangest imaginings: of flesh turned into atoms that drove before the wind, of stars flashing in their hearts, of cliff, sea, cloud and sky gathered together on purpose so that, out there, they might assemble the scattered pieces of the vision within. In those mirrors, the minds of men—in those pools of uneasy water, where clouds are always turning and shadows forming—dreams persisted. Every gull, flower, tree, man and woman, even the white earth itself, seemed to declare (though, if you questioned it, it would at once take the words back) that good triumphs, that happiness prevails, that order rules; and it was impossible to resist this strange hint. It was just as impossible to resist the extraordinary urge to roam this way and that in search of some absolute good, some crystal of intensity, far removed from familiar pleasures and known virtues—something alien to the business of domestic life, single, hard, bright, like a diamond in the sand, that would make its owner safe. Spring, meanwhile, had grown gentler and more yielding. english: Everything was silent. Nobody seemed to be stirring in the house yet. She looked at it, sleeping there in the early sunlight, its windows green and blue with the reflected leaves. The faint thought she was having about Mrs. Ramsay seemed in harmony with this quiet house, this smoke, this fine early-morning air. Faint and unreal, it was amazingly pure and exciting. She hoped nobody would open a window or come out of the house, but that she would be left alone to go on thinking, to go on painting. She turned to her canvas. But pushed by some curiosity, driven by the discomfort of the sympathy she was still holding in, unreleased, she walked a step or two to the end of the lawn to see whether, down there on the beach, she could see that little company setting sail. Down there among the little boats floating on the water, some with their sails furled, some moving slowly away, for it was very calm, there was one a little apart from the others. Its sail was being hoisted at that very moment. She decided that there, in that very distant and entirely silent little boat, Mr. Ramsay was sitting with Cam and James. Now they had got the sail up; now, after a little flagging and hesitation, the sails filled, and, wrapped in deep silence, she watched the boat make its way deliberately past the other boats and out to sea.

english: And what name would she give him? her father kept on. When he was a small boy he had had a dog called Frisk. She’s going to give in, James thought, watching a certain look come over her face, a look he remembered. They look down at their knitting, or something, he thought. Then all at once they look up. He remembered a flash of blue, and then someone sitting with him laughed and gave in, and he was furious. It must have been his mother, he thought, in a low chair, with his father standing over her. He began to hunt through the endless series of impressions that time had laid down on his brain, softly, ceaselessly, leaf upon leaf, fold upon fold: scents, sounds; voices, harsh, hollow, sweet; lights going by, and brooms tapping; the wash and hush of the sea; how a man had marched up and down and stopped dead, standing upright over them. Meanwhile, he noticed, Cam was dabbling her fingers in the water, staring at the shore, saying nothing. No, she won’t give in, he thought; she’s not like that. Well, then, if Cam would not answer, he would leave her alone, Mr. Ramsay decided, and felt in his pocket for a book. But she did want to answer him. She longed, passionately, to shift whatever lay on her tongue and blocked it, and to say, Oh yes, Frisk. I’ll call him Frisk. She even wanted to ask, Was that the dog that found its own way across the moor? But however hard she tried, she could think of nothing like that to say—something fierce and faithful to the compact, yet which would pass her father, without James suspecting, a secret sign of the love she felt for him. For as she dabbled her hand (and just then Macalister’s boy caught a mackerel, and it lay kicking on the bottom of the boat with blood on its gills)—for as she looked at James, who kept his eyes on the sail without any feeling, or now and then glanced at the horizon for a second, she thought: you aren’t exposed to it—this pressure, this split feeling, this extraordinary temptation. Her father was searching his pockets; another second and he would have his book. For nobody drew her more than he did. His hands were beautiful to her, and his feet, and his voice, his words, his hurry, his temper, his strangeness, his passion, the way he would say straight out in front of everybody, we perish, each alone, and his remoteness. (He had opened his book.) But what was still unbearable, she thought, sitting up straight and watching Macalister’s boy pull the hook from another fish’s gills, was that crude blindness and tyranny of his. It had poisoned her childhood and stirred up bitter storms, so that even now she would wake at night shaking with rage, remembering some command of his, some insolence: “Do this,” “Do that”; his domination; his “Submit to me.”

Nå, men hvis Cam ikke ville svare, ville han lade hende være, besluttede hr. Ramsay og famlede i lommen efter en bog. Men hun ville gerne svare ham. Hun længtes, lidenskabeligt, efter at flytte det, der lå på hendes tunge og spærrede, og sige: Åh jo, Frisk. Jeg kalder den Frisk. Hun ville endda spørge: Var det den hund, der fandt hjem over heden på egen hånd? Men hvor hårdt hun end prøvede, kunne hun ikke finde på noget af den slags at sige — noget heftigt og tro mod pagten, men som ville række hendes far, uden at James anede det, et hemmeligt tegn på den kærlighed, hun nærede til ham. For mens hun dyppede sin hånd (og netop da fik Macalisters dreng en makrel, og den lå og sprællede på bunden af båden med blod på gællerne) — for mens hun så på James, som holdt blikket på sejlet uden nogen følelse eller en gang imellem et øjeblik kiggede mod horisonten, tænkte hun: du er ikke udsat for det — dette pres, denne splittede følelse, denne ekstraordinære fristelse. Hendes far søgte i sine lommer; et sekund til, og han ville have sin bog. For ingen drog hende mere end han. Hans hænder var smukke for hende, og hans fødder, og hans stemme, hans ord, hans hastværk, hans hidsighed, hans mærkelighed, hans lidenskab, den måde han midt foran alle sammen kunne sige lige ud, vi omkommer, hver for sig, og hans afsides væsen. (Han havde åbnet sin bog.) Men det, der stadig var uudholdeligt, tænkte hun, mens hun satte sig op og så Macalisters dreng trække krogen ud af en anden fisks gæller, var hans rå blindhed og tyranni. Det havde forgiftet hendes barndom og vakt bitre storme, så hun selv nu kunne vågne om natten og ryste af raseri, når hun huskede et eller andet påbud fra ham, en eller anden uforskammethed: »Gør dét,« »Gør hint«; hans herredømme; hans »Underkast dig mig.«

english: Hares bored Minta, Lily thought. But Minta never gave herself away. She would never say a thing like that about chess in coffeehouses; she was much too self-aware, much too careful. Still, to go on with their story—by now the dangerous stage was behind them. Lily had stayed with them for a while last summer, and the car broke down, and Minta had to pass him his tools. He sat in the road fixing it, and the way she passed him the tools—businesslike, direct, friendly—was proof that all was well now. They were not “in love” anymore. No: he had taken up with another woman, a serious woman who wore her hair in a braid and carried a briefcase (Minta described her with gratitude, almost with admiration). She went to meetings and shared Paul’s views, which had grown more and more pronounced, on taxing land values and on a capital levy. That alliance, far from wrecking the marriage, had put it right. Clearly they were excellent friends, he sitting in the road and she handing him his tools.

Lily havde boet hos dem et stykke tid sidste sommer, og bilen var gået i stykker, og Minta havde måttet række ham hans værktøj. Nej: han havde slået sig sammen med en anden kvinde, en alvorlig kvinde, der bar sit hår i en fletning og gik med en dokumenttaske (Minta beskrev hende med taknemlighed, næsten med beundring). english: So that was the Rayleys’ story, Lily thought, smiling. She pictured herself telling it to Mrs. Ramsay, who would be eager to hear how the Rayleys had turned out. There would be a little triumph in it for Lily, telling Mrs. Ramsay that the marriage had not succeeded.

english: (All at once, as suddenly as a star slides down the sky, a reddish light seemed to blaze up in her mind; it covered Paul Rayley and poured out from him. It went up like a bonfire lit by savages on some faraway beach to mark a celebration. She heard it roar and crackle. For miles around, the whole sea ran red and gold. A smell like wine was mixed into it and went to her head, because she felt once more her own reckless longing to throw herself off the cliff and drown hunting for a pearl brooch on a beach. And the roar and crackle filled her with fear and disgust and drove her back. It was as if, even while she saw how splendid and powerful it was, she also saw how it fed on the treasure of the house, greedily and disgustingly, and she loathed it. Yet as a spectacle, as a glory, it outshone anything she had ever experienced; year after year it burned like a signal fire on a desert island at the sea’s edge, and you had only to say “in love” for Paul’s fire to leap up again at once, as it did now. Then it died down, and she said to herself with a laugh, “The Rayleys”—how Paul went to coffeehouses and played chess.)

english: Lily looked at the drawing-room step now. Through William’s eyes she saw the shape of a woman, quiet and peaceful, her eyes cast down. She sat lost in thought, pondering (she was wearing gray that day, Lily thought). Her gaze was lowered. She would never raise it. Yes, thought Lily, looking hard, I must have seen her look that way—but not in gray, and not so still, or so young, or so peaceful. The figure came easily enough. She was astonishingly beautiful, William said. But beauty wasn’t everything. Beauty had this price: it came too easily and too completely. It stopped life still—froze it. You forgot the small agitations: the flush, the paleness, some strange twist, some light or shadow that made the face unrecognizable for an instant and yet added something you saw in it ever after. It was simpler to smooth all that away beneath beauty. But what did she look like, Lily wondered, when she clapped her deerstalker hat on her head, or ran across the grass, or scolded Kennedy, the gardener? Who could tell her that? Who could help her?

english: She wanted to walk straight over and say, “Mr. Carmichael!” He would look up kindly, as he always did, out of his vague, smoky green eyes. But you only woke people when you knew what you wanted to tell them. And what she wanted to say was not one thing but everything. Small words that chopped the thought up into pieces said nothing at all. “About life, about death; about Mrs. Ramsay”—no, she thought, you could say nothing to anybody. The urgency of the moment always missed. Words fluttered off to the side and struck inches below the target. Then you gave up, and the idea sank back down, and you turned into what most middle-aged people become: cautious, secretive, with lines between the eyes and a look of permanent anxiety. Because how could you put these feelings of the body into words? How could you express that emptiness there? (She was looking at the drawing-room steps. They looked extraordinarily empty.) It was the body that felt it, not the mind. The physical sensations that came with the bare look of those steps had all at once turned extremely unpleasant. Wanting and not having sent a hardness, a hollowness, a strain right through her body. And then wanting and not having—wanting and wanting—how it wrung the heart, over and over! Oh, Mrs. Ramsay! she cried out without a sound, to that essence sitting by the boat, that abstraction made out of her, that woman in gray—as if to scold her for having gone, and then, having gone, for coming back. Thinking of her had seemed so safe. Ghost, air, nothing, something you could toy with easily and safely at any hour of the day or night—that was what she had been. And then suddenly Mrs. Ramsay reached out her hand and wrung the heart like this. Suddenly the empty drawing-room steps, the frill of the chair inside, the puppy tumbling about on the terrace, the whole wave and whisper of the garden, turned into curves and arabesques flourishing around a center of total emptiness.

Men man vækkede kun folk, når man vidste, hvad man ville fortælle dem. Og det, hun ville sige, var ikke én ting, men alt. Små ord, der hakkede tanken i stykker, sagde slet intet. »Om livet, om døden; om fru Ramsay« — nej, tænkte hun, man kunne intet sige til nogen. Øjeblikkets hastende karakter ramte altid ved siden af. Ordene flagrede til siden og slog ned nogle tommer under målet. Så gav man op, og idéen sank tilbage, og man blev til det, de fleste midaldrende mennesker bliver: forsigtige, hemmelighedsfulde, med rynker mellem øjnene og et udtryk af vedvarende uro. For hvordan kunne man sætte ord på disse kropslige følelser? Hvordan kunne man udtrykke den tomhed dér? (Hun så på stuetrappen. Den så usædvanligt tom ud.) Det var kroppen, der følte det, ikke sindet. De fysiske fornemmelser, der fulgte med synet af de nøgne trin, var med ét blevet yderst ubehagelige. At ville have og ikke få sendte en hårdhed, en hulhed, en spænding gennem hele hendes krop. Og så at ville have og ikke få — at ville og ville — hvor det vred hjertet, igen og igen! Åh, fru Ramsay! råbte hun lydløst til den essens, der sad ved båden, den abstraktion, der var lavet af hende, den kvinde i gråt — som for at skælde hende ud for at være gået og så, da hun var gået, for at komme tilbage. At tænke på hende havde forekommet så trygt. Genfærd, luft, intet, noget man let og trygt kunne lege med på ethvert tidspunkt af dag eller nat — det var, hvad hun havde været. Og så pludselig rakte fru Ramsay hånden ud og vred hjertet sådan her. english: And now, little by little, the pain of wanting, and the bitter anger (at being called back just when she believed she would never grieve for Mrs. Ramsay again—had she missed her among the coffee cups at breakfast? Not at all), grew less. What their anguish left behind, as a remedy, was a relief that soothed in itself, and also, more mysteriously, a sense that someone was there—Mrs. Ramsay, freed for a moment of the weight the world had laid on her, lingering lightly beside Lily and then (for this was Mrs. Ramsay in all her beauty) lifting to her forehead a wreath of white flowers and going off with it. Lily squeezed her tubes again and attacked the problem of the hedge. It was odd how clearly she could see Mrs. Ramsay stepping, quick as always, across fields that were soft and purplish in their folds, full of flowers—hyacinths or lilies—among which she vanished. It was a trick of the painter’s eye. For days after hearing of her death, Lily had seen her like this, raising the wreath to her forehead and going off unquestioningly across the fields with her companion, a shadow. The sight, and the phrase, had power to comfort. Wherever she was—painting here in the country, or in London—the vision would come, and her eyes would half close, searching for something to rest the vision on. She would look down the railway carriage, or the bus; take a line from someone’s shoulder or cheek; look at the windows across the way; at Piccadilly strung with lamps at evening. All of it had been part of the fields of death. But there was always something—a face, perhaps, or a voice, or a newsboy calling the evening papers, _Standard, News_—that pushed through, snubbed her, woke her, and demanded, and in the end received, an effort of attention, so that the vision had to be made again and again. Now once more, driven by some instinctive need for distance and for blue, she gazed down at the bay, turning the blue bars of the waves into little hills and the more purple patches into stony fields. And once again, as always, something that didn’t belong startled her. In the middle of the bay was a brown speck. It was a boat—she saw that after a second. But whose? Mr. Ramsay’s, she answered. Mr. Ramsay: the man who had marched past her, aloof, with his hand raised, leading a procession, in those beautiful boots of his, asking for sympathy she had refused to give. By now the boat was halfway across the bay.

english: Then the swirl around her hand died away. The water stopped rushing past; the world was full of small creaks and squeaks. You could hear the waves breaking and lapping at the side of the boat as if they lay at anchor in a harbor. Everything drew very near. James had kept his eyes on the sail until it had become like a person he knew, and now it sagged completely, so they came to a halt, flapping about and waiting for a breeze in the hot sun, miles from land, miles from the Lighthouse. The whole world seemed to stand still. The Lighthouse stopped moving, and the line of the far shore stayed fixed. As the sun grew hotter, they all seemed to draw very close together and to sense one another’s presence, which they had nearly forgotten. Macalister’s fishing line dropped straight down into the water. But Mr. Ramsay kept reading, his legs tucked up under him.

english: The book he was reading was a small, glossy one, its covers speckled like a plover’s egg. Every now and then, as they drifted in that dreadful calm, he turned a page. To James it seemed that every page was turned with a particular gesture meant for him—sometimes assertive, sometimes commanding, sometimes designed to make people feel sorry for him. And the whole time his father was reading and turning those little pages one after another, James was dreading the moment he would look up and say something sharp to him about one thing or another. Why were they hanging about here? he would ask, or something just as unreasonable. And if he does, James thought, I’ll take a knife and strike him to the heart.

english: This old symbol—taking a knife and striking his father to the heart—he had always kept. Only now that he was older, as he sat glaring at his father in helpless fury, it was not the man himself he wanted to kill, not that old man reading. It was the thing that came down on him—perhaps without his knowing: that fierce, sudden harpy with black wings, its claws and beak all hard and cold, which struck and struck at you (he could feel that beak on his bare legs, where it had struck him as a child) and then flew off; and there he was again, an old man, very sad, reading his book. That was what he would kill; that was what he would strike to the heart. Whatever he did with his life—(and he felt he might do anything, as he looked at the Lighthouse and the distant shore)—whether he went into business or a bank, or became a lawyer, or ran some enterprise, that was what he would fight, what he would hunt down and stamp out: tyranny, despotism, as he called it—forcing people to do what they didn’t want to do, taking away their right to speak. How could any of them say, But I won’t, when he said, Come to the Lighthouse. Do this. Fetch me that. The black wings spread; the hard beak tore. And then, a moment later, there he was, sitting reading; and he might look up—you never could tell—perfectly reasonably. He might chat with the Macalisters. He might be pressing a gold coin into the hand of some freezing old woman in the street, James thought; he might be cheering at some fishermen’s sports day; he might be flinging his arms about in excitement. Or he might sit at the head of the table without a word from one end of dinner to the other. Yes, James thought, while the boat slapped and lazed about in the hot sun: there was a wasteland of snow and rock, very lonely and stern; and there, he had begun to feel quite often lately, whenever his father said something that took the others by surprise, were only two sets of footprints—his and his father’s. Only they knew each other. Then what was this terror, this hatred? He turned back among the many leaves the past had folded inside him, peering into the heart of that forest where light and shadow so dapple each other that every shape is warped, and you stumble along, now with the sun in your eyes, now in dark shade. He was searching for an image that would cool his feeling, set it apart, and round it off into something solid. Suppose, then, that when he was a child sitting helpless in his baby carriage, or on somebody’s lap, he had seen a cart crush someone’s foot, without meaning to, innocently? Suppose he had seen the foot first, smooth and whole in the grass; then the wheel; then that same foot, purple and crushed. But the wheel was innocent. And so now, when his father came striding down the hall early in the morning, banging on their doors to get them up to go to the Lighthouse, it came down over his foot, over Cam’s foot, over anyone’s foot. You just sat and watched.

Det var det, han ville dræbe; det var det, han ville støde i hjertet. Hvad han end gjorde med sit liv — (og han følte, at han kunne gøre hvad som helst, mens han så på Fyret og den fjerne kyst) — om han gik ind i forretningslivet eller en bank, eller blev advokat, eller drev en virksomhed, så var det det, han ville bekæmpe, det, han ville jage og trampe ned: tyranni, despoti, som han kaldte det — at tvinge folk til at gøre, hvad de ikke ville, at tage deres ret til at tale fra dem. Hvordan kunne nogen af dem sige: Men det vil jeg ikke, når han sagde: Kom med til Fyret. Gør det her. Hent mig det der. De sorte vinger bredte sig; det hårde næb flåede. Han kunne stå og trykke en guldmønt i hånden på en forfrossen gammel kone på gaden, tænkte James; han kunne juble ved et sportsstævne for fiskere; han kunne slå ud med armene i begejstring. Eller han kunne sidde for bordenden uden et ord fra den ene ende af middagen til den anden. Ja, tænkte James, mens båden klaskede og dovnede i den hede sol: der lå en ødemark af sne og klippe, meget ensom og streng; og der, det var han for nylig begyndt at føle ret ofte, hver gang hans far sagde noget, der overrumplede de andre, var kun to sæt fodspor — hans og hans fars. Kun de to kendte hinanden. Hvad var så denne rædsel, dette had? Han bladrede tilbage blandt de mange blade, som fortiden havde foldet inde i ham, og spejdede ind i hjertet af den skov, hvor lys og skygge pletter hinanden så, at enhver skikkelse bliver forvredet, og man snubler af sted, nu med solen i øjnene, nu i mørk skygge. Han ledte efter et billede, der kunne køle hans følelse, sætte den på afstand og runde den af til noget solidt. Antag da, at han som barn, hjælpeløs i sin barnevogn eller på en andens skød, havde set en vogn knuse en andens fod, uden at mene det, uskyldigt? Antag, at han først havde set foden, glat og hel i græsset; så hjulet; så den samme fod, lilla og knust. Men hjulet var uskyldigt. Og derfor, når hans far nu kom skridende ned ad gangen tidligt om morgenen og bankede på deres døre for at få dem op til at tage til Fyret, så kom det ned over hans fod, over Cams fod, over hvem som helsts fod. Man sad bare og så på.

english: So this was the island, Cam thought, as she trailed her fingers through the waves again. Never before had she seen it from out at sea. So that was how it lay on the water: a dent in its middle, two sharp crags, the sea sweeping in there and stretching away for mile after mile on either side. It was tiny—shaped rather like a leaf standing on its end. So we took a little boat, she thought, and began telling herself an adventure story about escaping from a ship that was going down. But with the sea running through her fingers, and a sprig of seaweed disappearing behind them, she had no wish to tell herself a story in earnest. What she wanted was the feeling of adventure and escape. For as the boat sailed on she was thinking how everything had slipped away, passed, streamed off behind them: her father’s fury over the points of the compass, James’s obstinacy about their compact, her own misery. So what came next? Where were they heading? Out of her hand, icy cold, sunk deep in the sea, a fountain of joy shot up—joy at the change, the escape, the adventure (that she was alive, that she was here). And the drops from this sudden, thoughtless fountain fell here and there on the dark, drowsing shapes in her mind—shapes of a world she had not yet made real, turning in their darkness and catching a spark of light here and there: Greece, Rome, Constantinople. Tiny as it was, like a leaf on end, with the gold-flecked water flowing in and around it, did even that little island, she wondered, have its place in the universe? The old gentlemen in the study could have told her, she thought. Now and then she wandered in from the garden on purpose to catch them at it. There they would be (Mr. Carmichael, perhaps, or Mr. Bankes, very old and very stiff), facing each other in their low armchairs, crackling the pages of _The Times_ in front of them. She would come in from the garden with everything muddled in her head: something someone had said about Christ; a mammoth dug up in a London street; what had the great Napoleon been like? And they would take all this up in their clean hands (their clothes were gray; they smelled of heather), brush the scraps together, turn the paper, cross their knees, and every so often say something very short. As if in a trance, she would take a book off the shelf and stand watching her father write—so evenly, so neatly, from one edge of the page across to the other—coughing a little now and then, or saying something brief to the other old gentleman across from him. And standing there with her book open, she thought: here you could let any thought you had unfold like a leaf in water; and if it did well here, among the smoking old gentlemen and the crackle of _The Times_, then it was right. And as she watched her father writing in his study, she thought (sitting in the boat now) that he was utterly lovable and utterly wise; he was not vain, and he was no tyrant. Indeed, if he noticed her there with her book, he would ask her, as gently as anyone could, Was there nothing he could give her?

Den var bitte lille — formet nærmest som et blad, der stod på højkant. Lille som den var, som et blad på højkant, med det guldglitrende vand, der flød ind og rundt om den, havde selv den lille ø, undrede hun sig, sin plads i universet? De gamle herrer i arbejdsværelset kunne have fortalt hende det, tænkte hun. Nu og da vandrede hun med vilje ind fra haven for at tage dem på fersk gerning. Der sad de (hr. Carmichael måske, eller hr. Hun kom ind fra haven med alt i en forvirret bunke i hovedet: noget, nogen havde sagt om Kristus; en mammut, gravet frem i en gade i London; hvordan havde den store Napoleon været? Og de tog alt dette op i deres rene hænder (deres tøj var gråt; de duftede af lyng), strøg stumperne sammen, vendte avisen, lagde det ene ben over det andet og sagde engang imellem noget meget kort. Som i trance tog hun en bog ned fra hylden og stod og så sin far skrive — så jævnt, så net, fra den ene kant af siden over til den anden — mens han hostede lidt nu og da eller sagde noget kort til den anden gamle herre over for sig. Og som hun stod der med sin bog opslået, tænkte hun: her kunne man lade enhver tanke, man havde, folde sig ud som et blad i vand; og hvis den klarede sig godt her, blandt de rygende gamle herrer og raslen fra _The Times_, så var den rigtig. english: So a great deal depends, then, Lily Briscoe thought as she looked at the sea—hardly a stain on it, so soft that the sails and clouds seemed set into its blue—a great deal depends, she thought, on distance: on whether people are close to us or far away. For her feeling about Mr. Ramsay altered as he sailed farther and farther across the bay. It seemed to be drawn out, stretched thin; he seemed to recede more and more. He and his children seemed to be swallowed by that blue, that distance. But here on the lawn, right beside her, Mr. Carmichael gave a sudden grunt. She laughed. He clawed his book up off the grass and settled himself back in his chair, puffing and blowing like a sea monster. That was quite another matter, because he was so close. And then all was quiet again. Surely they were up by now, she thought, glancing at the house; but nobody showed. Then again, she remembered, they had always vanished the moment a meal ended, off on their own affairs. It all went with this silence, this emptiness, the unreal feeling of early morning. Sometimes things were like that, she thought, pausing for a moment to look at the long glittering windows and the blue plume of smoke: they turned unreal. It was the same when you came back from a journey, or got over an illness—before habit had spun its web across the surface again, you felt that same startling unreality; felt something rise up. Life was never more vivid than then. You could be at your ease. You did not, thank goodness, have to march briskly across the lawn to greet old Mrs. Beckwith as she came out looking for a corner to sit in—“Oh good morning, Mrs. Beckwith! What a lovely day! You glided, you shook out your sails (the bay was busy now, with boats setting out), between things and beyond them. It was not empty; it was full to the brim. She seemed to be standing in some substance up to her lips, to move in it, float in it, sink in it—yes, for these waters had no bottom. So many lives had spilled into them. english: Here on the grass, on the ground, she thought, sitting down and prodding a little colony of plantains with her brush, for the lawn was very rough. Here, sitting on the world, she thought. She could not rid herself of the sense that everything this morning was happening for the first time—perhaps for the last—just as a traveler on a train, even half asleep, knows as he gazes out of the window that he has to look now, because never again will he see that town, or that mule-cart, or that woman working in the fields. The lawn was the world; up here, on this high perch, the two of them were together, she thought, looking over at old Mr. Carmichael, who seemed to share her thoughts (though neither had said a word all this while). And perhaps she would never see him again. He was getting old. And he was getting famous too, she remembered, smiling at the slipper that hung from his foot. People said his poetry was “so beautiful.” They were bringing out things he had written forty years ago. There was a famous man now by the name of Carmichael, she thought with a smile—how many shapes one person could take on! In the newspapers he was that; here he was just as he had always been. He looked the same—a bit grayer, if anything. Yes, the same; and yet somebody had told her, she recalled, that when the news came of Andrew Ramsay’s death (a shell killed him in an instant; he would have been a great mathematician), Mr. Carmichael had “lost all interest in life.” What could that mean? she wondered. Had he gone marching through Trafalgar Square clutching a big stick? Had he sat alone in his room in St. John’s Wood turning page after page without reading a word? She had no idea what he had done when he heard that Andrew was dead, but she sensed it in him all the same. All they ever did was mumble to each other on the stairs, look up at the sky, and say it will be fine or it won’t be fine. That was how she knew him. She knew that something in him had changed. Not one line of his poetry had she ever read. Yet she felt she knew how it went: slow and sonorous, seasoned and mellow. It was about the desert and the camel, about the palm tree and the sunset. It was utterly impersonal; it had something to say about death and very little about love. He had a kind of aloofness. He asked very little of other people. Hadn’t he always lurched past the drawing-room window rather awkwardly, a newspaper under his arm, trying to dodge Mrs. Ramsay, whom for some reason he did not much like? Which was exactly why, of course, she always tried to make him stop. He would bow to her—pull up unwillingly and bow low. Irritated that he wanted nothing from her, Mrs. Ramsay would ask him (Lily could hear her) wouldn’t he like a coat, a rug, a newspaper? No, there was nothing he wanted. (Here he bowed.) Something in her did not appeal to him. Perhaps it was her masterful way, her certainty, a matter-of-fact streak in her. She was so direct.

english: During the war she had gone into a hall one day and heard him give a speech. He was denouncing something, condemning somebody. He was preaching brotherly love. And all she could feel was: how could he love humanity, this man who could not tell one picture from another—who had stood behind her smoking his shag (“fivepence an ounce, Miss Briscoe”) and made a point of telling her women can’t write, women can’t paint, not so much because he believed it as because, for some odd reason, he wanted it to be so? There he stood on a platform, lean and red and raucous, preaching love (among the plantains ants were crawling, and she disturbed them with her brush—red, busy ants, rather like Charles Tansley). From her seat in the half-empty hall she had watched him ironically as he pumped love into that cold space—and suddenly there was the old barrel, or whatever it had been, bobbing up and down in the waves, and Mrs. Ramsay hunting among the pebbles for her glasses case. “Oh dear! What a nuisance! Lost again. Don’t bother, Mr. Tansley. I lose thousands every summer.” At that he had pressed his chin back against his collar, as though afraid of seeming to approve such exaggeration—but he could put up with it from her, because he liked her—and had smiled very charmingly. He must have confided in her on one of those long excursions when people got separated and walked home alone. He was paying for his little sister’s education, Mrs. Ramsay had told her. It did him enormous credit. Her own picture of him was grotesque, Lily knew perfectly well, stirring the plantains with her brush. After all, half of what you thought about other people was grotesque. Such ideas served private purposes of your own. For her, he stood in for a whipping boy.
